findings.reason: The protected implementation is already the canonical interview solution. It derives the relevant width once, counts one bits per position, adds ones * (n - ones), and stores only conventional scalar state. The code is concise, immediately explainable, asymptotically optimal for reading the significant input bits, and has no naming or structural defect, so no candidate is justified.

Metadata consistently identifies public LeetCode problem 477, its Python integer-array method, and its runnable solve(nums) adapter. The implementation considers every unordered pair of array positions, counts each differing bit once, preserves duplicate occurrences as separate values, and returns the aggregate rather than individual distances.

The protected app source and immutable native source bound to verified submission 2064987196 are algorithmically identical: both derive width from the maximum value, scan each bit over all values, count ones with shift-and-mask, add the cross-group product, and return total. Their only differences are the native class wrapper and type syntax.

The legal 31-value, 127-value, and 511-value dense-bit workloads span more than 16x in the declared size and force all 31 bit-position scans. The exact current source passed all 10 opaque correctness executions and all three performance tiers at 0.98x the calibrated reference runtime. A correct pairwise XOR and population-count control passed every opaque output but failed only performance at 8.01x the reference runtime.

For n values and maximum significant width b, the implementation performs one n-value scan for each bit, giving O(n * b) time. The source bound nums[i] <= 10^9 makes b at most 30, and only scalar counters and loop positions are retained, so the manifest's O(1) auxiliary-space claim is exact.

The current-targeted Approach exactly derives the ones * zeros contribution, explains why summing independent bit contributions counts every pair distance once, contrasts the linear-per-bit scan with quadratic pair construction, explicitly defines n and b, and covers singleton, duplicate, all-equal, zero, and high-bit inputs.

The hash-bound modular Reference was checked directly against the live public statement. It preserves the Hamming-distance definition, all-unordered-pairs objective, both examples in order, Example 1's 0100/1110/0010 representations and complete three-pair sum, the absence of an Example 2 explanation, all three constraints including the 32-bit-answer guarantee, and the absence of visuals, tables, or later sections.
